maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT STRIKE SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Is the minister aware of the arrest in Montreal today -two hours ago, as a matter of fact-of Mr. Rene Levesque, a well-known television commentator, Mr. Jean Marchand, the secretary general of the C.T.C.C. and eight other prominent television producers, allegedly because they were singing "O Canada" in proximity to the Canadian Broadcasting Company's building in Montreal and refused to move?

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT STRIKE SITUATION
speechtext:
I am not aware of the incident to which the hon. gentleman refers. As I came into the house I heard that some difficulties had arisen outside the C.B.C. building in Montreal in which the Montreal police felt required to participate to some extent. I am not sure what arrests may have been made. If the hon. gentleman wishes I could go into the background of this affair in 30 seconds, and tell the house what has happened up to date. Perhaps I should bring

hon. members up to date on this question, anyway; I could have done so earlier, on motions.
I am advised by the C.B.C., that the situation in connection with this strike is something like Gaul; it is divided into three parts. The first part had to do with the strike of the producers to which frequent reference was made some weeks ago. I am speaking now from memory; however, four weeks ago, so I am advised by the C.B.C., an agreement in principle was determined between the producers and the corporation under which the producers might return to work. At that stage it developed that the producers felt they should not go back to work unless something was done on behalf of those who manned the picket lines.
Subsequent to that negotiations were carried on between the corporation and the union's representatives who had been on the picket lines. The first demand made was that they should be paid for the time they were on the picket lines. That was refused. Finally suggestions were made with respect to arbitration, and in the end those matters were settled.
As I understand it, on Saturday night- and again I speak subject to correction- agreements were arrived at between the corporation and all the unions under which those difficulties were settled, and then negotiations were again resumed yesterday between the corporation and the producers with respect to that agreement which had been entered into some weeks ago. Late last night it developed that there was some misunderstanding between the producers and the corporation as to the interpretation which was to be placed on one paragraph of that agreement. As a result the negotiations broke off either at a late hour last night or at an early hour this morning, and the representatives of the producers went back to Montreal to report to their associates there. I was advised that a meeting was to be held this morning at ten o'clock at which these matters were to be discussed.
That is all I know of this matter, Mr. Speaker, subject to the report I got just as I entered the chamber and the information given me by the hon. member in his question. I take it that the meeting was held this morning, and apparently after the breaking up of the meeting there was a demonstration of some kind in front of the C.B.C. building which resulted in some activity on the part of the police. I presume this will be a matter of news and doubtless it will be fully reported in the press. I shall certainly make inquiries as soon as I can, and I should be in
Inquiries of the Ministry a position to report to the house tomorrow giving all the details. That is all the information I have.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT STRIKE SITUATION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Did the C.B.C. give instructions to the police officers in Montreal to intervene in this matter, resulting in the arrest of these several distinguished people?

maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT STRIKE SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no knowledge of that whatsoever, but I would be very much surprised if a police force such as the police force of Montreal would take instructions from anyone as to what they think their activities should be.

maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT STRIKE SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question has to do with a radio report to the effect that the corporation would not recognize the producers' association if it was affiliated with the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour. Can the minister assure the house that this right of the producers will in fact be protected?

maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT STRIKE SITUATION
speechtext: I am not sure to what the hon. member refers when he speaks of the "right". The agreement which was entered into between the corporation and the union, each paragraph of which was initialled by the representatives of the union, I am told, provided explicitly that the producers would not become affiliated with any union whatsoever. That was the position which the corporation took from the beginning. It was well understood. I believe it is the position the corporation has taken throughout all these negotiations. It was felt that if the producers were to be recognized as a union they should apply to the Canadian labour board and obtain certification. I believe it was the interpretation of that clause of the agreement which caused the adjournment of the discussion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT STRIKE SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to ask a further question. In view of the statement made in the house on February 6 to the effect that the producers and the C.B.C. had arrived at an understanding-not an agreement, because one was not signed, but an understanding-can the minister tell the house or can he explain the reasons for the prolonged delay in reaching an agreement between those two parties?

maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT STRIKE SITUATION
speechtext:
As I explained, I thought, the reason is that after this understanding or agreement, call it what you will, was reached between the producers and the corporation, the producers then refused to go back to work until various unions which had supported them on the picket lines had, as they said, been looked after, so there were prolonged negotiations going on. Those on the picket lines first demanded that they should

Inquiries of the Ministry be paid for having marched around in the picket lines, or for having stayed at home when the picket lines were operating, and then finally the question of arbitration was discussed for some weeks. It was really a discussion not with the producers at all but with I think five other unions, three official unions and the artistes and authors who are not, as I understand it, officially recognized as unions but have been given the same status. Discussions were carried on with each of those five organizations during the last days or weeks, and they culminated only on Friday night or Saturday night when the producers came to discuss and, I am told the corporation thought, to sign the agreement which was entered into some time early in February.

maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT STRIKE SITUATION
speechtext: Perhaps the Minister of Justice will inform the house on what grounds or at whose request those respectable citizens were arrested this morning?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PRESENT STRIKE SITUATION
speechtext:
No,
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice is unable to inform the house because, after listening to the report of the Minister of National Revenue it appears that the arrests, if any, were made by the Montreal city police, which force is not subject to the authority of the federal parliament or government.

maintopic: COLUMBIA RIVER
COLUMBIA RIVER
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: COLUMBIA RIVER
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Public Works. My question is based on a newspaper report in the Vancouver Sun of February 26, of remarks made in the provincial legislature by Premier Bennett, concerning the development of the Columbia. The report reads as follows:
Ready to Go
On his recent trip to Ottawa Bennett said he met with federal works minister Howard Green and offered to sign an agreement now for public development of the Columbia with the federal government. Green would not support the plan, he said.
In view of the fact that the minister's statements in the house and in the country throughout the years have consistently indicated his constructive and co-operative approach to this question in order to clear up any misunderstanding would he care to comment on this report.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: COLUMBIA RIVER
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to the hon. member for Kootenay West for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question and for drawing the report to my attention. Like himself, I was amazed when I read that report, so much so that I am doubtful whether the premier of British Columbia actually made the statement. The facts are that the federal government has been and is very keen to see this development of the Columbia river go ahead and go ahead quickly. We have been somewhat concerned for fear the provincial government might have lost interest and turned its attention to the Wenner-Gren proposals for the development of the Peace river.
The hon. member will recall that in the statement I made on December 5, in my capacity as acting prime minister at the time, outlining the fact that we were suggesting to the United States that the question of downstream benefits should be referred to the international joint commission, I used these words among others:
Furthermore, the postponement of such development in favour of some other power scheme could well result in making the development of the Columbia river in Canada impossible.
I amplified that in speaking in the throne speech debate on January 29, when I said, as reported at page 512 of Hansard:
It is true that this project will depend upon the co-operation of the government of the province of British Columbia. They have been giving some indication that they would prefer to have a pet scheme of their own up on the Peace river developed by the Wenner-Gren interests. I can only say this. If this Columbia river project is killed by failure of the government of British Columbia to co-operate they will be doing a great disservice to the people of our province and to the people of Canada.
With this background I met with Premier Bennett here three or four weeks ago-and by the way he also met with other ministers. I asked him as to whether or not his government really intended to do anything about the Columbia river. The hon. member knows that Premier Bennett is a very impetuous and, might I say, impatient man. He said, "Why, let us sign a letter of intent right away". Of course neither of us was in a position to sign a letter of intent, and I pointed this out to him. If he did make the statement referred to, this can be the only justification he had for making it, which I suggest amounts to absolutely no justification at all.
Actually the international joint commission met about two weeks ago in New York and had a very successful meeting. They are meeting again later in March at Chicago. The policy of the federal government remains as it was set out in the speech from the throne on October 14, 1957, namely:
Inquiries of the Ministry
My ministers are pressing for a favourable settlement of international problems in connection with the Columbia river to clear the way for a joint program with the province of British Columbia to develop the immense power in the waters of this river.
In addition to the meetings of the international joint commission, a technical committee has been set up consisting of representatives of the province of British Columbia and the dominion government. This committee has met twice and had very useful meetings. I believe a higher level committee with representatives from the two governments is also to be set up. There is every reason for hope that there will be full cooperation in the early development of the Columbia river. Certainly there will be no lack of co-operation on the part of the federal government.

maintopic: COLUMBIA RIVER
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I want to thank the minister for clearly removing any reasons for misunderstanding and establishing the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite evident that the hon. gentleman has quite misapprehended the situation. Members of the tariff board are appointed for ten year terms. The one qualification laid down by the Tariff Board Act is that a member reaching 70 years of age retires automatically. It happens that the terms of the two vice chairmen of the tariff board expire on March 31 next. That is all there is to the matter. Their terms will expire on the 31st day of this month.

If he continued on the board he would reach the point of retirement, because of the 70 years of age provision, in about two years, I believe. But Mr. Hector McKinnon, than whom there is no finer or more highly respected public servant in this country, had decided, I am informed, well over two years ago-certainly a considerable time before this government came into office-that he did not intend to wait until he reached 70 years of age before retiring, and he had communicated that wish to my predecessor, who urged him to carry on.
Shortly after the present government took office Mr. McKinnon intimated to me that he wished to retire shortly. He gave me the reasons. I assure the house that the reasons are entirely personal. No significance should be attached to this matter on any other basis whatsoever. In view of the heavy docket of cases and references awaiting decision on the part of the tariff board, it was at my urgent request that Mr. McKinnon agreed to carry on. He has extended the period that he had agreed to carry on, and at the time of the last extension I made it a matter of a strong request to him that he should carry on until
Inquiries of the Ministry completion of the report of the board on a particular reference.
At some personal sacrifice and by changing plans he had made, Mr. McKinnon accommodated that wish, and out of a sense of public duty he agreed to carry on until March 31 and is doing so. In so doing he is earning the warm-hearted gratitude of the government.
I wish to say that I greatly regret that Mr. McKinnon is not carrying on until he reaches 70 years of age. However, the decision he has made is one that I must respect and accept. When he agreed to the last extension I promised that I would not ask him to carry on beyond March 31 because of the fact that he was yielding to some considerable pressure on my part in agreeing to carry on until March 31.
I leave this subject, Mr. Speaker, with this observation. I think Mr. Hector McKinnon, in the long years of service he has given to the people of Canada in a variety of responsible positions in the public service, has earned the undying gratitude of all Canadians.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion to go into supply provides me with the opportunity to raise certain questions concerning defence policy and defence planning in this country, with special reference to the necessity of planning defence production. I express a hope at once, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Defence Production will follow me immediately in order to deal with the questions in regard to this matter which I propose to raise. We have not heard from the minister on this matter Mr. Speaker. I know, he will be happy to take advantage of the opportunity we are now giving him.
As I have just said, Mr. Speaker, I propose to make special reference to the necessity of planning defence production in order to avoid in the future such wasteful, confused and harsh procedures as those which were followed in the cancellation of the contract for the CF-105. As we are now entering into a new era of defence policy, of defence production, and I hope of defence organization in this country, in view of changing circumstances it is all the more important, surely, that the government should adopt businesslike and efficient procedures, planning and development, among other things, to ensure that our defence production and defence activities do not become mere adjuncts to those of the United States.
Defence Policy, Planning and Production
The defence activities, defence plans and defence policies of our two countries are bound to be very closely related. No one on this side, Mr. Speaker, desires to do or say anything which would interfere with the necessity of defence arrangements which recognize the interdependence of the two countries; but while that surely is obvious and inevitable, the recognition of interdependence in defence matters must be a genuine recognition of genuine interdependence, and not the subordination of these matters of arrangements for the production and the planning of one country to those of the other. No one emphasized the necessity for Canada maintaining her own position within this context of interdependence more than hon. gentlemen opposite when they were sitting on this side of the house.
I should like at the beginning to look at the air defence situation with regard to policy and planning. When the government took over in June, 1957 one of the very first things it did in this field was to agree to the establishment of a North American air defence command after what we have always, on this side of the house, considered to have been quick and casual consideration. As has been made very clear in this house during previous sessions, this was done without any formal intergovernmental agreement and without referring the matter at the time to parliament. The speed with which Canada's air defence squadrons were put under this North American command was quite a contrast to the delay and uncertainty with regard to government policy respecting the Arrow contract.
I suggest that the strong and obvious desire of the United States government at that time to set up NORAD gave the Canadian government a great opportunity to ensure that Canada's legitimate rights in all aspects of continental defence should be safeguarded and ensured. We had a very high card to play in the negotiations which then took place, and it was a Canadian card which could have been played without prejudicing continental security in any way. Indeed, it might have been played in a way which would have increased continental security because, notwithstanding what the Minister of National Defence has said in this house, the United States and Canadian air defence commands at that time were very closely co-ordinated even in the absence of an agreement such as the NORAD agreement. We certainly were not standing alone at that time. This was the opportunity to have made our views known to the United States and to have laid down reasonable conditions which would have strengthened and maintained the Canadian position without interfering in any

Defence Policy, Planning and Production way with legitimate demands for continental security which, of course, must always come first.
What should we have done on that occasion? I suggest that in the first place we should have pressed for the placing of NORAD under NATO command, for NORAD becoming part of the Atlantic effort, and as genuinely collective in that regard as SACEUR and SACLANT.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: You are a little late.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The hon. member says we are a little late. This matter was brought to the attention of the House of Commons and to the attention of the public almost as soon as the NORAD agreement was published; and at that time, one and a half years ago, we suggested that the arrangements should be made part of NATO. I made reference to this matter not only in the House of Commons but also in the country before the house met.
The other thing which I suggest should have been done at that time is this. We should have linked the signing of the NORAD agreement with suitable and equitable arrangements for pooling defence production and developing defence resources. We know what happened. Those things were not considered at that time, or if they were considered nothing was done about them, and as a consequence of the signing of the NORAD agreement, desirable though it may have been in other respects, any subsequent room for manoeuvre in order to protect our Canadian position in continental defence was very greatly weakened.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow a question? He has mentioned what the effect would have been if NORAD had been, as he suggested, made part of NATO. I am not going to discuss that question or agree with him for a moment in his contention in that regard, having already taken an opposite position. But I would ask him what possible benefit that would have had-even if he be correct in his conclusion-having regard to what happened in the signing of NORAD, in bringing together a stronger sense of joint production. Did we achieve anything in that direction when we joined NATO?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The Prime Minister did not quite follow what I was saying. Perhaps hon. members opposite would permit me to make it clear. I showed the courtesy of permitting a question to be asked, and I hope hon. members opposite will show me the courtesy of allowing me to reply.
I said two things might have been done at that time. One was that we might have made NORAD a command of NATO. I said
that without any reference to the pooling of defence production or the development of defence resources. I said that the second thing which might have been done at that time-and I am not relating this to NATO- was to have linked the NORAD agreement, irrespective of its relationship to NATO, with suitable arrangements for pooling defence production and developing defence resources. That was when we had the opportunity to bring these two things about.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Was the same opportunity not available when NATO was set up?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I would remind the Prime Minister, though I am sure he does not need any reminder, that under the NATO pact, the tenth anniversary of which we shall be celebrating in a few weeks there were clauses designed to bring that about. Article 2 was one, and there are others. And at the first meeting of the NATO council a committee was set up to implement those clauses and put into effect the principle of balanced collective forces. But this was studied, and this was done, only in respect of the western European part of NATO defence, because the North Atlantic sector was not included in NATO at that time. Perhaps that should have been done when the commands were set up. In so far as it was not done the former government, naturally, takes its share of the responsibility. However, there was another opportunity when the United States expressed its wish to establish a North Atlantic defence command, and that was done-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Had his government not been negotiating with the United States about the setting up of NORAD, and had it done anything about this pooling of production?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman raises a perfectly fair question. It is usually put in the form, did you not agree to NORAD before 1957? This, as I have said more than once, was not the case, and I am on record as saying so at half a dozen places in Hansard. Consideration of the NORAD agreement in 1957 did not proceed to the point where the cabinet took any decision with regard to it. The matter was still under consideration by the departments most concerned. The Department of National Defence, I admit, had one view with regard to the advisability of signing this agreement at once. Other departments of government-and I can perhaps include myself as the head of one such department-felt that before such an agreement was signed, with all its far-reaching consequences, every implication should be studied, and one implication was the effect upon joint production and the development

of our resources. That was still under consideration when the government changed.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Is there any record of that view on your part?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
My hon. friend has the departmental records at his disposal, and I have some records of memoranda at my disposal. I can assure my hon. friend that if there had been unanimity in regard to this matter at the time, and if it had been discussed and decided not as it was later in 1957-at one or two cabinet meetings at the most, it would have been done; but the fact that it took so long to do it shows how seriously it was regarded by us as a change in Canadian defence and defence production policy.
What was the situation, then, in regard to the planning and development of the CF-105 when the new government took over? The Minister of National Defence has emphasized on more than one occasion that there was no immediate change and that the government decided to carry on, as the previous government had carried on, by reviewing the matter from time to time, I believe every six months or every year, and that that procedure, proceeding from stage to stage, would be carried on as of the summer of 1957.
The minister also informed us last week and indeed earlier that during the summer of 1957 some extremely significant changes took place in the strategic conditions which govern defence policy, and indeed that is undoubtedly the truth. There were three such changes that had a direct bearing, surely, on any government decision in regard to proceeding with or discontinuing the CF-105 contract. One of those changes which altered the whole world strategic picture was the firing by the Soviet union on August 27, 1957 of the first intercontinental ballistic missile. The other two changes both took place on October 4, 1957. One was the unveiling by the A. V. Roe Company of the first Arrow as a completed machine or, if you like, a going concern which made it possible in a way which was not possible before for the government to negotiate for its sale to other countries. The other change was perhaps the most far-reaching of all and it occurred, as I said, on the same day, October 4, the day the Arrow was unveiled in Toronto. On that same day the Soviet launched its first earth satellite.
The minister is quite right in stressing the importance of these developments, as he has done more than once, on the strategic picture in the world and indeed on the strategic picture in regard to our own defence policy and planning. Presumably the government took notice of these developments, but presumably also it decided at that time, in the
Defence Policy, Planning and Production autumn of 1957, to carry on for another year with the Arrow proceeding from stage to stage and reviewing the progress after each stage.
In view of what happened in the autumn of 1957 I suggest that was the time for the government to have come to certain decisions, not a year and a half later. In view of the fact the minister said only last week in this house that these developments represented very significant changes in the strategic scene, I suggest the government should have acted at that time. Those changes took place in the autumn of 1957, but it was not until February of 1959 that the government took definite if negative action with respect to our air defence planning which the minister argued the other day was required by, among other things, the changes I have jusl mentioned.
The minister will surely agree with me- and if he does not he will perhaps interrupt me and tell me-that the strategic situation as it developed following the changes I have mentioned made it quite clear, as he himself has already indicated, that the number of CF-105's needed would be far less than the 500 originally estimated as required for Canadian squadrons. If that was true it was bound to mean that there would be a very great increase in the cost of the CF-105 development unless we could sell some of these planes abroad. Therefore I ask what should the government have done in the autumn of 1957?
Surely the government should have tried to secure an order from the United States. Surely it should have endeavoured to secure a definite decision from the United States at that time as to whether or not an order was forthcoming, and in the light of what it learned from Washington then to decide before the end of 1957 whether it should gradually wind up the CF-105 project after working out alternative ways of using the productive facilities of the company, or whether it should go ahead and build the number required, which we later learned was 100, and during that period until completion, which we are now told would have taken to the summer of 1961, plan for the future use of these air production facilities.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the government did not do either of these two things in the autumn of 1957. The minister has told us that the first approach by a minister of the present government to the United States government for an order was not until September of 1958, about 10 months later. Indeed, at his press conference on television last Tuesday, February 24, the minister-and I quote from the record of that conference-had this to say:
It was only in December-

Defence Policy, Planning and Production
That is, December of 1958.
-that we got the final definite "no" when we were over in Paris that the United States would not take it.
By "it" the minister meant the Arrow, of course. He then went on to say:
I got the impression-
I emphasize that word "impression".
-when I went down to Washington in the fall-
That is the fall of 1958.
-that the United States were not interested in it and then at that conference of ministers in Paris I asked for a definite decision.
In other words the minister asked for a definite decision not in December of 1957 but in December of 1958.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: The hon. gentleman invited me to interrupt, and perhaps I could do so at this point. If I could not get a definite decision in September of 1958, how could I get a definite decision in September of 1957?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I do not know, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Nor do I.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: But surely the minister, who is an experienced man in these matters, could have gone down to Washington in the autumn of 1957 and told the United States government, "If you cannot give us a definite decision one way or the other we will have to plan without taking your needs into consideration at all". Did the minister have to wait from June of 1957 until December of 1958 to find out from the United States whether or not they would buy the Arrow?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: He did not wait that length of time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: What did he do?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: The dates speak for themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Why did not your government see what it could do about selling Arrows to the United States before it got into this big program?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
That is an easy question,
because it has been asked and answered before. As the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence have said, the minister of national defence of that time, almost as soon as the Arrow was in a stage of development that would make it possible to talk about, went down to Washington and received what the minister described the other day as an encouraging response. How could he sign up the United States or ask the government of that country for a definite decision negatively or affirmatively before the first Arrow


had been completed? No government is going to buy a plane on the drawing board; but the plane had come off the drawing board on October 4, 1957.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Yes, but it had not flown.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: It flew in March of 1958. If the minister is the forceful military diplomat we know he is, surely there was time to find out after October of 1957 what were the intentions of the United States government in this matter.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: May I answer that question? They were anxious to see performance in the air before they made a decision.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
It was March, 1958 when it performed in the air; but the government claims now that it acted wisely and it acted well in abandoning the Arrow in the middle of February, 1959, and in planning after the event what should be done to cushion the resulting dislocation and sudden and serious unemployment.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, there is no possible justification for that kind of procedure, which is a sorry example of the lack of decision and lack of planning on the part of the government. Every argument the government now advances merely points up first that the government should have got that decision from the United States long before February, 1959. And if that decision had been negative, then the government should have made up its mind. If the decision it made was against putting the CF-105 in production, then the government, and not in the third week of February, should have planned alternative production policies and made orderly arrangements for change with the company, and incidentally saved the taxpayers millions and millions of dollars.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that we have the right to draw it to the attention of the house. The matter was allowed to drift and no final decisions were taken until February, 1959. During those months the government itself had not made up its own mind finally whether or not manned interceptors were considered to be essential in the light of the conditions as they developed. I refer the minister to his own statement in the House of Commons last January. I refer him, as I have referred him before-indeed, I have put them on the record-to his statements in the estimates committee in July, 1958, which undoubtedly encouraged the view that the CF-105 was to be continued; or, if it was not to be continued, that its place would be taken by some other manned interceptor and that Bomarcs were merely supplementary.
I think what has already been put on the record from this side has clearly shown that

this was the impression the government desired to create in the country. There is much additional evidence to confirm that view. The Minister of National Defence is reported in the Calgary Herald of January 18, 1958, over a year ago, as saying:
I do not share the opinion that the Arrow will be obsolete before it is operational. When Russia stops building bombers it will be time for us to start thinking of some other defence.
Russia has not yet stopped building bombers. Somewhere along the line in the last 12 months there has been a change in government policy and attitude in regard to the value of manned interceptors, and particularly in regard to the value of the CF-105. But, Mr. Speaker, the government now says we did plan; that we did plan ahead. The Prime Minister told the house and the country that he told the company last September that the contract was over, and therefore the corporation is to blame for not minimizing the effect of that decision on employment or for making the necessary readjustments. Well,
I have no brief for this particular corporation, but I suggest to the Prime Minister that this is a most unfair charge against the company in view of what actually happened.
The Prime Minister rests his case for the attack he made on the company not so much on the text of the September statement, to which reference has been made more than once, but on the interpretation given to that statement in press clippings. Well, I can produce as many clippings as the Prime Minister produced to show that other interpretations were given by other newspapers. But let us return to the text of the statement itself. I know it is ambiguous, All you have to do is read it to realize that it is ambiguous, but these particular words are not so ambiguous; and I quote from the statement:
The government has decided that the development program for the Arrow aircraft and the Iroquois engine should be continued until next March-when the situation will be reviewed again in the light of all the existing circumstances at that time.
The Minister of National Defence confirmed that last Monday when he spoke in the House of Commons and on the same day the Prime Minister attempted to create, from his reading of newspaper clippings, the opposite impression. The minister said on that day, a week ago today, that permission had been given last September to extend the development for a further period to try out certain changes in the interests of economy. At the same time that statement was issued, or a day or so later, Mr. Gordon of the A. V. Roe Company had this to say, and I quote from his statement:
We anticipate no change in the level of operations.

The Prime Minister said a week ago that there was a death sentence at the end in September, and the corporation should have known. The Minister of National Defence took a very different view a couple of months later. This is another example of confusion and contradiction, Mr. Speaker, in regard to important policies. But I suggest that even if there had been-let us admit for the purpose of argument that there had been- a clear and final notice of cancellation given to the company in September to take effect later, the position of the Prime Minister and the government in this matter is even worse; because in spite of that clear and final notice which they claim they gave, they ignored completely the A. V. Roe proposals for other projects and other work made last November. If the Prime Minister had indeed cancelled the contract, as he said he had, in September, it is utterly incomprehensible that those proposals made by the company should have been ignored by the Prime Minister or the government, especially in the light of that hidden report which we mentioned this afternoon of the air industries and transportation association, presented to the government as far back as September 2, 1957, which indicated some of the consequences to the air industry of developments that were occurring, and which was also ignored by the government.

Moreover, as one of my colleagues will show in detail in this debate, the procedure regarding cancellation of contracts embodied in government regulations left the company with no alternative but to act as they did on the abrupt notice that they received. They were told by telegram, "The contract is over." There was no other work that they had to perform except that under this contract for the government. Yet they were expected to continue operations when the contract had been taken away from them.
Where is the evidence of defence planning in this situation? If in fact the government had decided last September to cancel, consultations should have taken place at once with the representatives of the company to plan ahead, at the very least, to discuss the company's own proposals. We are not alone in questioning the wisdom of the procedure followed by the government in this matter. Apart from all the criticisms that have appeared in various Canadian newspapers regarding this procedure and the way this was done, perhaps I might quote a paragraph from the London Times of last Friday which had this to say:
It has been known for six months that the Arrow would probably have to be dropped-
That is as far as the London Times goes.
It has been known for six months that the Arrow would probably have to be dropped; what the friends of Canada would like to see is more evidence than has yet appeared that the government and the company have spent the interval in fruitful consultation on the best means of lessening the impact of the impending blow-and it is from the government that the initiative should be expected.
In the eyes of the government all the initiative in this matter was to have come from the corporation which had this contract cancelled without the kind of warning that we suggest should have been given. This is just further evidence to support our major indictment of the government that it refuses to face a problem until it becomes a crisis and then acts piecemeal and in panic. In this important matter that is the record, a record of inadequate and inefficient planning.
However, the decision has now been taken. Perhaps in the long run equally important, if not more important, is the question, where do we go now? On what concept and strategy is our defence policy now to be based? What is to be our relationship to the United States and also to NATO in regard to the implementation of this policy? Strategic conditions, the minister says, and he is right, have changed in the last few years. They have changed drastically. The missile has arrived. We are told that the Soviet union will be operational intercontinentally in this field of destruction and


diplomatic pressure by the middle of this year. We are told that by a high officer of the pentagon in Washington.
So we are now in outer space with all of its implications for war and for peace. What then should be the defence policy, the defence planning, the defence production policy of a country in Canada's position in this new strategic era? Should we not at this time be reviewing our whole concept of defence planning? I hope that in this debate the government will throw some light on this vital question which is more than ever in our minds now that Canada has abandoned one sector of the defence front in so far as domestic production is concerned, that sector being the production of Canadian manned interceptors, and has changed to United States produced missiles.
Surely in the light of this change, with all of its implications, we should have a hard and long look at our air defence policy and Canada's part therein. What effect should this change and the reasons for it have on defence planning? Are manned interceptors now obsolete? Only a short time ago the government rejected this view but it seems now to agree with it. If the word "obsolete" was not used in the house a week ago the impression certainly was given that the CF-105 could not do the job now for which it was designed in the light of changed circumstances. If the CF-105 is obsolete, then all manned interceptors in service, about which we know anything at the present time, and especially the CF-100, must be considered obsolete. Yet the CF-100 is our only equipment in Canada at the present time in the field of manned interceptors.
What is the policy now? Surely the maintenance of the CF-100 which is obsolete-there can be no argument about that in the light of the weapons it might have to meet-and the introduction of the Bomarc represent not so much a change of policy as a makeshift expedient until a policy is worked out. Perhaps the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) will have something to say about that. The minister made what I thought was a very important and rather strange statement the other day when he said in the house, as found on page 1283 of Hansard for February 23, that even if the CF-105 is ended-and it is now ended-and if the CF-100 is not adequate-and of course it is not adequate for the purposes for which it was designed-we can rely on the United States manned interceptor defence and provide additional facilities for them to operate, if necessary, over our country.
I ask the minister this question. Does that mean that we are going to give up our own

R.C.A.F. squadrons once the CF-100 is finished and we are not producing it any more, or what does it mean? Has this part of air defence by manned interceptors now been assigned to the United States air force operating, if necessary, as the minister put it, over our country, which I take it would mean operating from Canadian bases? If that is not the interpretation, if that is not the meaning, are we not moving in that direction? Is the role of the R.C.A.F., with CF-lOO's and not CF-105's now minor and secondary in continental defence to an extent greater than ever before, even though we all know that the R.C.A.F. will, as it always has, carry out whatever role it is given with skill and devotion?
There is another question which has a very direct bearing on this matter. Is any provision being made for the manufacture of these United States manned interceptors in Canada? If we are going to depend more and more on the United States for manned interceptors have we made arrangements or are we contemplating arrangements for these interceptors to be used in Canada to be manufactured in Canadian factories and give work to those production facilities which have now been rendered idle by the cancellation of the Arrow?
Then there is another question. What is our position in Canada with regard to missile defence development? Let me quote what the Minister of National Defence said the other night over the air ii a press conference. He said:
I think we have got to get into that field-
That, Mr. Speaker, is the field of missiles.
-and if we stay back too long we'll be left out.
Again, he said:
We've got to get in on the ground floor . . . and use our scientists to help in planning.
Incidentally, with regard to the use of our scientists to help in planning, the current defence research estimates having to do with defence planning have undergone a very large reduction. But the minister said, "We have got to get in on the ground floor and use our scientists to help in planning." How are we going to use them? By planning for United States manufacture? It would appear so judging from recent developments.
Mr. Speaker, this is not a question of manned interceptors versus missiles and their relative value in the light of the threat they have to meet. Only experts can decide that matter. It is a question-and we have to decide it in this House of Commons-of Canada's role now that the decision has been taken to abandon the manufacture of our own manned interceptors and to introduce
Defence Policy, Planning and Production missiles and to store nuclear warheads for those missiles on Canadian territory under United States jurisdiction and custody, something which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) told the committee on external affairs last summer was not under consideration. There has obviously been a change in policy there.
The way in which these Bomarcs, and the Sage which goes with the Bomarcs or vice versa, are being introduced into continental air defence in Canada, appears to make us completely dependent on United States equipment, technology and supply. Surely it was not the intention of the Minister of National Defence in what he said over the air the other night to suggest that Canada was going to enter into the missile field in this way and surely that is not the way in which we should enter that field if we are going to enter it at all. These Bomarcs are made in the United States. They are being supplied to R.C.A.F. squadrons for Canadian use at Canadian stations which are under Canadian command and they are paid for by the United States. I refer to the equipment, the Bomarc itself. I suggest, as I have already stated in this house, that this is the first time in our history that we have accepted what we used to call in the war "lend-lease" from the United States. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) tries to dispose of the argument by saying that we are doing that, not only two-thirds to one-third, but we are letting the United States pay all the cost of the D.E.W. line and we are letting them.

The minister will have a chance to speak later, Mr. Speaker. The minister must know that all during the war we managed to look after our own expenditures with regard to Canadian services activity and I say that we can do it in the future. The wheel has gone full circle. In 1912-13, the Conservative government of the day proposed to give dreadnoughts to the British fleet and opposed the Liberal policy of establishing a Canadian navy. In 1959 we received for R.C.A.F. squadrons missiles from the United States.
Will the government tell us something about their policy with regard to this missile development? These Bomarcs, whatever their effectiveness may be now-the Prime Minister merely says that the range of action, whatever it may be, is comparable to that of the CF-105-will undoubtedly soon be obsolete and will have to be replaced. Are we to continue to rely on the United States to provide, at United States expense, all the subsequent air defence missiles we require and pretend that it is a Canadian contribution? If not and if we avoid what I consider to be this mistake in the future by taking on the full financial responsibility for our own R.C.A.F. squadrons, may we not be

getting into a field that will turn out to be as expensive as the development of the CF-105?
If it is unwise to continue production of weapons which do not meet according to the government, our military requirements the alternative, the purchase-or even their receipt as a gift-of weapons in the United States which may soon be obsolete surely would be worse. The first at least provided employment and engineering development in Canada. But the second merely reinforces our dependence for production, technology and policy decisions on the United States. In puts us in the position of having to accept or refuse what the United States is going to make available to us. For manned interceptors our dependence on the United States is now absolute.
We are entitled to ask the question, is it to be the same for missiles in spite of the brave words of the Minister of National Defence the other night that we must enter into this missile field? Is the conclusion now inescapable that the continental air defence system is now under the control and organization of the United States for planning, for production and for operation? The production of the CF-100 is ended. The Astra and Sparrow projects have been terminated. The CF-105 has been abandoned; and the report of the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) tabled last week in this house does not give us too much encouragement that we are going to participate in continental air defence production jointly with the United States except with regard to contracts which cover part of a greater United States effort. We have learned that there is very little to be hoped for from other NATO countries.
Therefore I ask the question, can we expect this Canadian segment of defence industry to expand, or even to survive, as an adjunct to a United States industry when it would be dependent on the consideration of the United States government or the generosity of the United States producers? How can the scientific and technological research, which the minister rightly thinks are essential, but the appropriations for which have been drastically cut this year, develop in Canada in such circumstances?
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that these are all-important questions which should be answered in the course of this debate. I suggest that recent decisions of the government also make necessary an immediate and basic reappraisal of the whole defence situation to see what we can best do now in the changed circumstances to protect our national interests, while making our most effective Canadian contribution to the collective effort for
Defence Policy, Planning and Production security and peace. What about the radar detection and early warning system? Even in the present strategic position-I know the Minister of National Defence will agree with me on this-it could not be of more importance in so far as bombers are concerned. We must have an effective early warning system to give the retaliatory air forces of the United States strategic air command time to get off the ground and on their way to the enemy target. This after all is our strongest protection now against all-out assault, because it is our strongest deterrent.

continental defence, and that is the best procedure for its own defence. In doing that there are certain things which the United States has to do which we cannot do, and we should not lose sight of that fact. I was beginning to say that we should be careful before we get into this new field of missiles, which the Minister of National Defence said we must enter on the ground floor, so that we may learn about all its implications in terms of strategy and economy. Now, after this diversion, I am going to-

I am one of those who feels that if we can afford to take over activities on our own soil which are now being done by someone else-in this case the United States-we should do so. Therefore the question arises, which I have asked more than once: Should we so adjust our defence planning and defence policy to take over the operation of the D.E.W. line? What would that mean in terms of expenditure? Similarly, what would taking over the Pinetree line, or that part of it which is now operated by the United States mean, in terms of expenditure? There is a strong argument, I suggest, to the acceptance of Canadian responsibility here. I am quite sure that the government is not likely to do that, and they should not do it without finding out exactly what they are taking over. Perhaps the minister will be able to give us some information on that score, because we are told- when I say we are told, we are told from public sources-that the present D.E.W. line will soon be quite obsolete, even against the newest, most modern bombers; and in so far as intercontinental ballistic missiles are concerned it will only give a few minutes' warning.
Therefore, if we do decide to take over this line, would we be taking over what has been called an airborne Maginot line, which may have been essential and which was effective a couple of years ago-but a lot has happened in the nature of the threat to

this continent in the last two years. What has been the effect of these developments on the D.E.W. line and on the Pinetree line and what changes will be required in order to make the D.E.W. line effective to meet this threat? Some astronomical figures have been given out in Washington regarding the amount that would have to be spent to make this line effective. What are the implications for Canada in a situation which goes beyond the D.E.W. line and into an early warning system against the missile, with an antimissile missile behind it?

Perhaps never before in air defence history-and I will restrict it to air defence history-has such a review been more greatly needed. And if anything were needed to underline the necessity for this kind of review it has been the procedure adopted by the government in the past week in

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION

Mr. Speaker, at 2.30 this afternoon I was feeling in good spirits and good health. I am not quite certain how I feel at the moment. The whole issue is undoubtedly an important one, and I know it to be a most confusing one. The problems which must be resolved in order to arrive at an effective air defence policy are, indeed, vastly complex.
They are so complex that it is necessary almost to think in terms of social economy, the budget, industry, national theories and international theories in order to arrive at a conclusion which is most likely to lead to the achievement of what we all desire, namely the maintenance of peace and the satisfactory air defence of this country.
We all know that over the years Canada has been making very heavy defence expenditures. I think it is important that we should try to start at the very beginning and follow the situation through if we hope to arrive at any reasonable and logical conclusions. In view of the fact that we are spending hundreds of millions of dollars annually through the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production it seems reasonable to ask ourselves this question: why are we making these expenditures? I think it is fair to say that our heavy defence expenditures are necessary only because of fear of aggression, to prevent aggression or to protect Canada as fully as possible in event of aggression. I believe it can be said that Canada is making these expenditures because of fear of a possible war.
If we concede that we make heavy expenditures for defence because of the fear of possible aggression then it seems only natural to consider what kind of aggression it is against which we are trying to defend ourselves. All present indications are that there can be only three types of aggression, either all out thermonuclear war, a limited nuclear war or a conventional war. It could only be one of the three.
Aggression in the form of an all out thermonuclear war can only come about either 

through a miscalculation or through desperation and would undoubtedly be mutual suicide for those concerned. As far as Canada's air defences are concerned we will surely all admit we have neither the knowledge, equipment or resources to defend ourselves in the event of an all out thermonuclear invasion. I believe we find ourselves in a similar position with respect to a limited nuclear invasion. It seems logical to conclude that a limited nuclear invasion would have almost as serious results for Canada as an all out thermonuclear invasion and indeed it would undoubtedly lead to an all out thermonuclear war.
In view of this situation there can be no question but that Canada finds itself in a most difficult and vulnerable position partly because of power politics as they are being played today. As has already been pointed out and as is in the knowledge of all our members Canada is a country that is small in population but large in territory. We must be factual and honest in assessing the situation. We in Canada would be in the position of being in a no-man's land, if I may use that term, should a conflict develop between the United States and the U.S.S.R.
I was interested in the brief remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) with reference to the relationship of Canada to NORAD and of NORAD to NATO. We reiterate what we said here a year ago when NORAD was under discussion, that in our estimation NORAD should have been part and parcel of NATO. There should have been full integration and full partnership. We are more than ever convinced of the correctness of our position at this time. I believe that had that policy been pursued a year ago Canada today would be in a far stronger position to go to the United States and discuss proper terms of relationship and partnership in the production of defence materials. It would not have been in the position of an under-populated country talking to a powerful neighbour nation; it would have the voice and authority of all the countries that make up the organization of NATO. We in this group feel a very serious mistake was made a year ago and we are beginning to learn some of the results today.
I was interested in hearing the Leader of the Opposition use the word "planning" as often as he did in the course of his remarks.
I believe he was absolutely correct in emphasizing the need for planning with respect to our defence situation. The present condition that exists in our defence has come about as a result of a lack of planning. Because of a lack of economic, social and defence planning we find ourselves today in a predicament involving what almost amounts to the closing

down of factories and actual hardship imposed on thousands of workers who are now unemployed.
Of perhaps even greater significance-important as the other factors are-is the fact that the unplanned approach to the question of defence has resulted in confusion being confounded. An analysis of the statements made by the Prime Minister and other members of the government on the question of defence if put all together represent a highly contradictory series of statements and conclusions. One just cannot make any kind of sense from the type of information that is given to this house and the people of Canada with respect to defence in general and air defence in particular. We had an announcement on the part of the Prime Minister concerning the cancellation of the contract for the construction of the CF-105. The hon. gentleman made it clear time after time that the basic reason for the cancellation of the contract was that the threat of aggression by bombers had greatly lessened and that in view of the potential type of aggression possible today the CF-105 was completely obsolete and therefore, heartbreaking as it was, the government had to reach that conclusion.
If that statement was correct-and we had to accept the statement as being correct- what is the point of spending $350 million on the purchase of Bomarcs? As I understand it the Bomarc is no defence against an ICBM but is against the bomber. If the manned interceptor, even as up-to-date a manned interceptor as the CF-105, is no longer required because we will not have to face aggression by manned interceptors-using the Prime Minister's approach-then it is just as ridiculous to purchase Bomarcs because surely they are just as obsolete as the CF-105. Why cancel the expenditure of $400 million or $450 million which would provide work in Canada and instead spend $350 million in the United States on a weapon that is just as useless and obsolete as the Arrow is considered to be?

We have to go beyond the situation which has developed because of the cancellation of the CF-105 and the purchase of the Bomarc to consider other angles where the defence air has to be cleared by the government.
As I mentioned before, it is not good enough for the Prime Minister to tell us that the CF-105 contract is cancelled because the manned interceptor is no longer of use and is obsolete, and he is going to buy the Bomarc which is obsolete except that it is not manned, and not explain the position and the decision of his government in relation to the other countries of the western powers. If it is correct that the day of the manned interceptor is gone and the manned interceptor is obsolete, then this house is entitled to know, if the decision of Canada is the correct one, why is it not the decision of the United States? If the decision is the correct one for Canada and the manned interceptor is no longer needed for continental defence, will the Prime Minister explain to us why in the budget introduced only two weeks ago in Great Britain they allocated hundreds of millions of pounds for new manned interceptors? If it is necessary there and our decision is correct, then why is it that West Germany has placed a contract for the renewal of parts and engines for their manned interceptors?
We hear a great deal of the dangers and the serious critical situation surrounding West Berlin. Canada has squadrons there equipped with the CF-100. Are we leaving them there with the CF-100? In the event of an attack are we leaving them there with something which is completely obsolete? These various things put together, just do not make sense, and at least I understand why the Leader of the Opposition asks so many questions. This confusion needs to be cleared away. It can only be cleared away by the contradictory statements being expunged and the house given information as to why various countries have differing policies.
We are all interested in the same thing, namely the maintenance of peace and the protection of our own country. I also feel that a few things must be said on the particular air defence situation in regard to Canada and our relation thereto with the United States.


According to the government's declaration, Canada is no longer going to produce manned interceptors. Moreover, we are no longer going to equip our squadrons with manned interceptors. We are not going to produce the new types of defensive weapons which modern defence makes absolutely essential. That can only mean, therefore, regardless of our interest in continental defence, that we are placing the main, if not the whole, responsibility on the United States. This means, whether the government likes the term or not, that because we are not in the major field of production any more, because we are not even going to produce the defensive armaments that we hope to have, because we are not going to be able to continue the work of scientific production in the greater fields of defence against nuclear or thermonuclear aggressive weapons, we have handed over a great part of Canadian sovereignty to the United States. This becomes of particular note when we remember the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) that the retention, possession and control of all nuclear warheads will remain with the United States. There is something that has always puzzled me, especially in view of the statements made by cabinet ministers opposite that the threat now is the ICBM. I understand that these missiles will travel 12,000 to 15,000 miles per hour and have a range of 5,000 to 6,000 miles. That means that if we are going to be able to shoot them down we have to be mighty fast. Suppose we do have a retaliatory or defensive weapon. What are these ICBM's going to do? Are they going to remain motionless in the air until we can collect warheads from the United States wherever they may have them in order to shoot down ICBM's travelling 12,000 miles an hour?
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) was taken aback a little the other day when he was asked a question about a statement made by a Conservative member of parliament in Great Britain who used to be deputy commander of the NATO Atlantic fleet. That gentleman said that although he was second in command of the NATO fleet in 1952 he did not know where the atomic warheads were kept and if anything had happened to the supreme commander he would not have known what to do because he did not know where the warheads were and did not know who could tell him. I suppose he would have just waited until he found out where they were.
I think we are in a somewhat similar position in Canada. Even if somebody in Canada does know where the warheads are or will be, unless they are right where the defensive weapon is they are not going to

be of any use against an ICBM. It may be that for security reasons the government does not give us more information. But, as I said before, until the government does give us more information there is going to be a continuation of confounded confusion or confusion confounded. That is not fair to members of the house when they have to vote hundreds of millions of dollars for two departments because members of the house have a basic responsibility for Canadian defence policy and the question of where control lies.
There can be no question that we have to enter into a partnership in respect of continental defence but it is of the utmost importance that it be a true partnership, an honest partnership, a partnership on the basis that Canada is not just permitted but is expected and given every opportunity to collaborate and work on scientific projects and to produce not just a few small parts but to make a major contribution in the production of those things that will be used to mutual advantage in continental defence. It is absolutely essential for the maintenance of our economy and productive capacity and the maintenance of our scientific and technical personnel that such a true partnership should be brought about.
I have no hesitation in saying that the government should be most roundly and soundly condemned for taking the action they took the other day without at least having some definite agreement with the United States on these matters. Why, the situation was positively farcical. "Farcical" is the only word I can think of to describe it. We were told that the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) would be making a major speech in which he would tell us all about the situation. But when he got up and made his speech, Mr. Speaker, it was not a matter of a balloon being pricked; there was just no balloon to prick. How he spoke with pride of the $1,700,000 contract obtained by one company to build a wing or some other part of the Bomarc missile.
Surely when the government was faced with having to make this most important and far-reaching announcement, which extends far beyond the laying off of 14,000 or 30,000 men, a statement which means a complete revision and alteration of Canada's whole defence policy, the government should have taken far greater strides and reached far greater objectives in negotiations with the United States on the question of production in Canada and the holding together of our scientific and technical personnel. From the inefficiency and ineptitude of the government it would almost appear that they had in the 66968-9-96J
Defence Policy, Planning and Production back of their minds the handing over of the sovereignty of Canada to the United States.
