Mr. Speaker, I will deal first
with one slightly unrelated remark which was made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). He said it did not make sense to him that the United Kingdom should be developing manned interceptors at this time while Canada was not going ahead with the development of the CF-105 or words to that effect. I think that is a correct interpretation of his remark. The reason is of course this. The great bulk of the Russian bomber force is made up of short-range bombers, sometimes referred to as medium bombers. These are not capable of travelling from Russia to the North American continent-Canada or the United States-turning around and going back again. However, they are quite capable of going from Russia to the United Kingdom. If the Russians wanted to start a war, surely they would use that type of bomber against targets which were within the range of that bomber. Therefore the United Kingdom, with their Royal Air Force, must be prepared to meet that threat. That is a threat which is not serious against this continent because the range of those medium bombers would not allow them to come and attack targets here but it does allow them to attack targets in the United Kingdom. I think that should answer the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East.
The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) raised a number of questions. I will endeavour to answer them in some form of sequence, but it is not easy to do so because they were not in a definite logical order as they were put to the government. First of all, he queried national defence policy. National defence policy is based on our external affairs policy and it goes back to 1950. In 1950, at the time the Korean war broke out, Canada and the other countries which had the same desire for peace and democracy, bound themselves together in a solemn covenant that they would stand united against any aggressor. We have adhered to that policy which, by the way, was initiated by the Liberal government. There has been no fundamental change in that policy since the change of government. We believe it is imperative that we stand together with the other countries in what has now become known as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and that we recognize as a solemn


obligation the agreement that, if any one of them are attacked by an aggressor, the attack will be met by the combined effort of all NATO countries. That is the fundamental policy behind our endeavour to give peace and security not only to this country but to the rest of the world.
Now a word as to the application of that policy. The plan for the application of that policy has been drawn up by commanders from the different countries meeting together as an advisory council. The policy of NATO is to provide, first of all, a shield which is partly in Europe and partly on this North America continent, in order to protect, first of all, those powers of retaliation which are the second half of the NATO defence concept; second to gain sufficient warning in Europe or on this continent to make quite certain that any advances made by the aggressor are of sufficient strength to warrant the full response of our retaliatory forces; and third, as far as Europe is concerned, if possible to delay the advances of any ground forces so that the countries of western Europe are not overrun. I think you might say that these are the main duties of the shield element of NATO.
As to the strike-back element or the powers of retaliation, they consist of the United States bombers, the British bomber force of the R.A.F. and also such missiles as may be in location in Europe at the present time. That is the force of retaliation. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this policy has held good and has prevented war for the last ten years and more. The proof of the soundness of this NATO policy is the peace which the western world has enjoyed all during this time. When people ask you what you have to show for these enormous expenditures on national defence, the answer is that you have enjoyed peace ever since NATO has been formed and that no territory has been taken away from any NATO country since it was formed. To support NATO in a balanced organization is the defence policy of this government and it will continue to be the defence policy of this government.
When NATO was first set up it was decided that there should be an integrated balanced force, not each country having a little balanced force of its own but a balance of the collective countries of NATO, each country contributing to that integrated or balanced force the particular type of weapons or manpower which that country with its resources could give and which was dictated by the element of geography. So we see now an attempt which has been growing, getting stronger and more closely co-ordinated every

year, leading to an integrated balanced force available for the defence of the western world.
We have to keep adjusting the type of forces which we are providing and the type of assistance which we are giving to the western world. We have to adjust the help which we are giving in other channels, not only that related to armed forces but also in the channels of diplomacy and our contribution to the welfare of underdeveloped countries. All of those things are part of the deterrent; they are part of the effort being made to prevent the spread of communism.
Periodically we have to consider the changes which have to be made in our approach to this problem in the type of weapons which we are providing, the numbers of troops which we may have available for any particular task. I do suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we are living today in an era of extremely rapid advances in science and technology. I am not ashamed to say that some of the programs which appeared to have great merit only twelve months ago no longer have the same importance of urgency in view of progress made on more technically advanced projects. We have to review the situation continually. Continually we are trying to see where the threat lies and what are the best means to counter that threat. Science is not standing still. Science is producing innumerable new developments, and the armed forces must adjust their programs and equipment to the advances made by science. It is so easy to have said twelve months ago, "You should have done this", or "You should not have done that". If we were planning against an enemy who was kind enough to inform us exactly what was in the inventory of his armament, it would be very much easier than trying to guess what a possible aggressor might do when the means of obtaining information are extremely limited and are not available immediately there is any change in the would-be aggressor's plan of armament and organization of his forces.
I therefore suggest that it is no discredit to any government if they are cautious at times and want to be perfectly certain before they take some particular line of action, and if they try to be as near certain as possible that that action is right. When this Avro Arrow program was started, I mentioned the other day that the Right Hon. C. D. Howe said it made him shudder that it was expected he would have to spend possibly $100 million, as he put it, "of other people's money". It is no easy responsibility to shoulder when instead of $100 million you are faced with the possibility of having to spend on one single project $781 million of other people's money,
Defence Policy, Planning and Production who will hold this government responsible if that money is not wisely spent.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the government is charged with the responsibility of providing the best defence it can, within the limitations of the money that is available without ruining the economy of this country, so that the people of our country can live in peace and security. If we let our armour down we would be blamed. There probably would not be very many people left to blame, but it is a responsibility which we have to face, and we are conscious of that day in and day out. You are not going to discard some particular form of development which only a few months ago looked to be a very encouraging and worthwhile project to pursue.
In 1957 we assumed office, in June, without the knowledge which had been accumulated in the years before. We had to take advice from the service chiefs who had studied this problem continually, and they were then of the opinion that we should still go ahead with the development of the Avro Arrow. After the government had been in power only a few short months we made the decision to go ahead with the development of the Avro Arrow for one more year. That recommendation was made with the advice of the service chiefs. The same men, with one exception, are our chiefs of staff today. They had the courage, when new light was brought on a possible threat, to change their recommendation in this respect. They had the courage to advise the government that the nature of the threat had changed, that they had consulted with their opposite numbers in other countries and were convinced that there was a change in the degree of the threat. That recommendation was given only late last year.
There has been some suggestion to this effect: "Why did you not go to the United States as soon as you were elected to office and tell them that they had to buy the Avro Arrow?"

In the fall of 1957 the Avro Arrow had just come out of the work shops. One of these Avro Arrows was available for inspection on the runway. It did not come out under its own power; it was dragged out on a tractor. There were United States officers present, and they were very impressed with the look of the Avro Arrow; I understand they reported back to their superiors in Washington that the Arrow had great promise. And in the fall of 1957 there was very little change in the United States attitude toward this machine which had been indicated to my predecessor, the Hon. Ralph Campney, when he went down to Washington and when he was given encouragement to go ahead with the Avro Arrow, no commitment being made. And we were given encouragement to go ahead with the Arrow in 1957 because the United States thought it might be the answer and they might have to adopt this aircraft. I went down in the fall of 1958, and by that time the opinion of senior officers of the United States air force was changing, and they were becoming doubtful.
In Paris, as I said, I got an indication that the United States was no longer considering any possibility of adopting the Arrow, but it was not a firm decision at that time, and no firm negative was expressed. It was not until December of last year when we were in conference at a meeting of the two groups of ministers that they said once and for all that they would not take the Avro Arrow. It is so easy to think that everything is black and white and that one can go down and talk with a group of statesmen from another country and get a definite yes or no on the very first visit, before they have even made up their own minds.

In September there was, as I said, an indication that the United States would not take it. That indication, or that assumption on my part, was confirmed in December at the Paris conference. It was clear enough in my mind, although it had not been formally stated; it was clear from conversations I had had with various air force officers and others that it was very unlikely at that time that the United States would proceed with the Arrow. Hon. members must remember that it was only a week ago that we received a final and definite note from the United Kingdom on this matter.
During all these months we had been approaching officials, governments and ministers both in the United States and in the United Kingdom to see whether there was any possibility of interesting them, or any other of our NATO partners, in the CF-105. I think it is clear, therefore, that we were making efforts to interest other countries in this project, and that until the fall of last year it was impossible for this government to have made any decision about the continuance of the Arrow. It was about the same time that this government, the government of the United Kingdom and the government of the United States were able to reassess the threat which they considered would most likely come from any aggressor.
What is that threat? As I said in answer to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver East, the threat to the United Kingdom is still considered to be a threat by manned bombers as well as by missiles, the reason being, as I said earlier, because of the range of the majority of the manned bombers in the soviet armament inventory.
Now with regard to the threat to Canada. In the past, as I said last week, we had anticipated a big build up of Russian long range bombers capable of attacking targets on this continent and returning to airfields inside the Soviet union. That threat does not appear to have materialized, and according to the best information that it is possible to secure

Defence Policy, Planning and Production
it is thought that the Russians are not building up long range bomber fleets but are turning their effort into that of producing missiles rather than bombers. Hon. gentlemen opposite have asked why, if we are going in for Bomarcs, the United States and ourselves are still keeping in operation such interceptor aircraft as the CF-100, the F-101, the F-104 and the F-106 in the United States air force. The reason is that for the next few years if the Russians intended to attack this continent it is reasonable to think that they would put into operation the intercontinental missiles which they have, and that they would also, in all probability, put into operation such of their bombers as they might be able to spare for targets better within the range of the bombers that they possess. So we believe we had better keep a defence against these bombers which might be used against this continent although they would not be considered as the main arm of the aggressor. They might well come over and take on secondary targets or targets which had escaped attack by missiles. Therefore, it is surely wise to keep a certain number of interceptor squadrons for that purpose.
The United States is reported in the press as having some 70 squadrons of supersonic interceptors available for the defence of the North American continent. We have 9 squadrons of the CF-100. People ask the question whether the CF-100 and the Bomarc are obsolete. They are not obsolete as long as the Russian bombers exist. The moment the Russians scrap their bombers they will become obsolete. The moment the Russians place their whole dependence upon the missile attack then the Bomarc and the manned interceptor will become obsolete but as long as there is a bomber in the Russian air force which is capable of coming to this continent and back, or is capable of coming to this continent and being scrapped here we should still keep our interceptors in the form of our CF-lOOs which are quite capable of dealing with the majority of Russian bombers.
The interceptor squadrons of the United States air force, some of them being supersonic, are of course in a more advanced stage of development than our own CF-100. That is one of the advantages that flows from entering into an alliance or an agreement to produce balanced forces. All countries do not have to have equipment which is produced to meet the threat at exactly the same time.
A couple of years ago when the CF-100 was coming into operation Canada had the best all-weather interceptor on the North American continent. The United States did not have as good an aircraft as we had. The
United States has caught up for the time being and they have an interceptor and a means of intercepting Russian bombers superior to the CF-100. In the NORAD agreement about which some remarks were made this afternoon it is written that the squadrons of either side may for a short period or may temporarily move across the boundary and in order to facilitate that there will be certain developments made at some of our air fields particularly in western Canada where we have no defence provided by the R.C.A.F. It is outside of the range of the CF-100 or the CF-105 and so we rely today upon squadrons of United States air force to provide protection against enemy bombers over a large portion of Canada. I hope that clears up the question of obsolescence. The CF-100 will become obsolete when the Russians remove their bombers from the inventory they have.

Defence Policy, Planning and Production was laid then on the importance of interdependence, not only interdependence in the use of weapons but interpendence of production. The Leader of the Opposition asked whether we could take over the D.E.W. line. It would cost us between $30 million and $40 million annually, but as approximately 90 per cent of the employees are Canadian one might query whether that would be a good move.

Mr. Speaker, before the house rose for the dinner recess, the Leader of the Opposition had asked for information with regard to the cost of the Pinetree system. As I explained, the Pinetree system is shared by the United States and by Canada, some of the stations being operated by Canadians and some being operated by the Americans. That figure of $43 million includes some $5 million which the United States are spending on purchasing equipment for those stations in Canada.
Hence if Canada were to take over the operation of the line in its entirety it would mean the addition of $43 million to our defence budget at the present time. I put in


that qualification "at the present time" because additional equipment is being provided for these radar stations in order that their range and control may be improved. There are always advancing techniques in this field of electronics. If we are to keep up to date and if we are to increase the scope of these radar stations we must put in the additional and new equipment.
Questions were asked with regard to the D.E.W. line and I made some reference to the extent to which Canada was assuming more responsibility for the administration as well as the operation of D.E.W. line stations. In order to round off that part of the statement I had made I think it might be of interest to hon. members who had made inquiries about this development if I were to state that the Department of Transport plans to take over the administration and operation of some seven air fields on the D.E.W. line. This taking over will not be done overnight, but in two or three years' time I hope that we shall be operating those stations.
One of the biggest difficulties that has existed for those people who wished to go into the Canadian Arctic and to utilize such facilities as have existed in the past at the D.E.W. line air fields has been the lack of accommodation. Naturally when the Federal Electric Company, which is carrying out the administration of the D.E.W. line, established their stations it was agreed that they would not be required to provide unlimited accommodation for those persons who for other purposes than those connected with the D.E.W. line might be visiting the north. As there has been in recent months a phenomenal interest shown in our Canadian Arctic more and more people may be expected to move into those far northern regions. Therefore the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources are making plans to construct accommodation at the principal D.E.W. line stations so that Canadians who are visiting the Arctic will no longer be required to obtain accommodation in the quarters of the Federal Electric Company. That accommodation will be a great convenience to the many prospectors, engineers and scientists of oil companies and so on who are developing the potential wealth of those Arctic islands. Hence we have the Department of Transport and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources both co-operating in, may I say, the maintenance of Canadian sovereignty in the far north. Everywhere you go at all these stations on the D.E.W. line you now see the scarlet coat of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refute emphatically the suggestion that defence policy is muddled and confused. I recall the fact that only last week a similar amendment was moved in the House of Commons in Westminster, and there the opposition also accused the government of not having any defence policy. Our defence policy is based on the recommendations which are made by the chiefs of staff of our armed forces, and I would like to say here that there is no group of officers more loyal than those who comprise our own chiefs of staff. They are a devoted band of capable and experienced men dedicated to the service of this country. They are not only men who have had actual experience in recent operations, in command and in staff duties, but they are also a forward-looking group who are trying to provide us with the soundest advice that is possible for any group of officers to give. They are confronted with almost insurmountable difficulties. They are trying to peer into the future, trying to keep up with the advance of science, but they are resolving those problems.

Defence Policy, Planning and Production
Again I must insist that our defence policy is perfectly clear. Furthermore, it has proved effective. Through collective agreements we contribute to the integrated balanced forces of the free nations, thus preserving peace by the twin media of the shield and retaliatory forces of NATO. In Europe our troops share the responsibilities with those of our allies in preventing the western countries from being absorbed by communism. On this side of the Atlantic navy, army and air force have the double task of protecting our own country and that of providing security to the forces of retaliation so that they, in their turn, may be an adequate deterrent to any enemy. If the deterrent should fail to deter the would-be aggressor we shall endeavour to provide the best means we can for the survival of our nation under the nuclear attack which is bound to follow any act of madness that might plunge the world into another global conflict. As far as policy is concerned I assert that there is no confusion.
Regarding the program for the provision of forces and their armament to give implementation to this policy, this program must be flexible. Because of the improvements in technique and the advances of science, because of changes which may be introduced in the armament inventory of a potential aggressor, as well as the long period of time that must elapse between the inception of a modern piece of equipment until it comes into operational use, I fear there is a possibility that programs may in the future be changed, perhaps before some of the projects have been completed. Rigidity in this respect would be fatal. On Friday last the Prime Minister clearly outlined the principles associated with defence, and the broad basis of our program. There was no confusion in his thinking. He made it perfectly clear that caution will be used in defence expenditure; courage when a hnal decision is required.

For almost thirty minutes he put on the record all of the things that had been done in order to obtain contracts and in an effort to get work in substitution for that which had been stopped. But with what results? He said they were not successful, notwithstanding all of the effort expended in this direction.
It occurs to me that this is one area in which the minister should have been successful but perhaps there is a reason why the government, the minister and those associated with him were not successful in obtaining these orders. If the minister was right in the fact that these difficulties arose around the middle of October of 1957, then we know what was happening at that time. The government was getting ready for another election. Ministers on the other side of the house stated repeatedly that the session at that time was nothing more or less than a preparation for the next election so it is no surprise to us on this side of the house that perhaps the government was not paying the attention that it should have paid to matters of this importance.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION

Mr. Speaker, I rose not so much to deal with that aspect as to deal with the defence production aspect of this contract and if the house will be good enough to listen to what I have to say there are two or three points I should like to make before dealing with this question in particular.
At the outset I should like to say that in my view the decision which was made to produce the Arrow was a sound one. I do not believe there is any disagreement with that statement in the house. I believe, too, there is agreement that under the circumstances in which the country found itself at that time the decision to develop that aircraft taken in 1953 was justified from a military standpoint. There is also another point that is consequential upon that one and it is this. That decision meant that the Canadian aircraft industry would continue to develop after having succeeded in producing the CF-100 which had proved so effective. This meant more employment opportunities and also an increasing number of skilled personnel and research personnel working in Canada in fields that are vitally important for our future technological and industrial programs.
During the post-war period the aircraft and allied industries had become a major sector of the Canadian economy. It was therefore also sound for the government to develop the CF-105 on a tentative basis. I repeat again that I do not think there is any disagreement on this point and it was my impression that the Prime Minister was in full agreement with that position when he spoke the other evening. However, as was pointed out by the Minister of National Defence, the Leader of the Opposition and others, the launching of the first earth satellite by the Russians on October 4, 1957 was a basic factor which should have affected our air defence policy because it was quite clear at that time that a new era was beginning, that of the intercontinental ballistic missile.
What did the government do? The Minister of National Defence complains about the fact that we on this side of the house say the government did nothing. Well, if the minister objects to that form of accusation let me say this to him. At least for a period of a year, from that time until the statement was made to the press in September 1958 by the Prime Minister, certainly there had been no indications given to the public or to the house that anything was being done. If there is a complaint because of that perhaps it is, as has already been stated on a previous occasion by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), that at about that period and


to a large extent still the views of the Canadian government were not received too sympathetically in the United States. I need not quote some of the things that were said during a former debate-I would be out of order-or some of the things said by the press, in an effort on my part to embarrass anyone. In view of statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite during two election campaigns in connection with our subservience to the United States in other fields, surely it cannot be objected to now when we say what I have just affirmed that we are complaining unduly about the conduct of our friends on the other side of the house.
However, it is a fact that in October of 1957 a new situation existed because of the Russian satellite orbiting the globe. We also knew then that we would need less of these aircraft than the 500 or 600 to meet our requirements. We further knew that the cost of producing the aircraft added a great deal to our defence requirements and that that might be well beyond our financial capacity unless, of course, Canada were successful in selling these aircraft to the United States.
It was one year later that the government decided to discuss that possibility in accordance with what has already been said. If these discussions had been initiated earlier or immediately after the events following October 4, 1957, when the CF-105 was unveiled and the Russians launched the satellite, the results probably would have been entirely different. I say that the delay between October of 1957 and September of 1958 in reaching a decision was completely unjustified. If the government is right now in abandoning the CF-105 it could and should have reached that decision if not a year and a half ago at least a year ago after the second election and saved about $200 million of the taxpayers' money. However, the issue was allowed to drift.
Statements made by the Minister of National Defence in July indicated that at that time the government certainly had not faced up to the situation. It was only in September of 1958 when the Prime Minister issued his first statement to the press that the government gave some indication it was at last considering this problem.
Now, if I may take a moment I should like to say a word about the statement made by the Prime Minister during the debate which took place here last Monday. It seems to me that if the Prime Minister had followed the tactics of the Minister of National Defence in giving to the house his version of the events and the facts instead of throwing the blame for this whole matter on the company it would have been far better not only for the

Prime Minister but for the country as a whole. The Leader of the Opposition said earlier that he had no mandate to defend the company and neither have I, but I do want to say without hesitation that the attack which was made on the company in my humble opinion was not only improper and unfair but it was unwarranted.
It was contended during the course of the debate that the press release of September 23, 1958 made it clear that the government intended to cancel the CF-105 at that time. I am not going to put on Hansard the words which the Prime Minister quoted himself because the Leader of the Opposition has already done that. I am not going to go into the fact that for quite a lengthy part of his speech the Prime Minister quoted press statements to the effect that his statement was clear and did indicate a cancellation at that time. However, in order to substantiate my argument, I shall quote just the last sentence of the press release which was made by the Prime Minister in September 1958 and which is as follows:
The government has decided that the development program for the Arrow aircraft and Iroquois engine should be continued until next March, when the situation will be reviewed again in the light of all the existing circumstances at that time.
Surely these words are clear; surely they mean exactly what they say and I do not see how they could be interpreted by anyone, certainly not by the company, to mean that the CF-105 was abandoned and that it was the intention of the government to cancel its production at that time. I say, further, if you go along with the Prime Minister and assume that he was right and that that statement did give an indication of cancellation, which I deny, then does the house, does the minister, does the government think that that is the way in which to sever the relationship between that aircraft company and the government? Surely that is not the way to operate as between government and industry in this country.
Listen to what the president said in his statement to the Globe and Mail the day following the announcement made on February 20. He said:
The Prime Minister's announcement cancelling forthwith the Arrow and Iroquois programs came as a complete surprise to the company. We received no advance notice whatever of the Friday announcement itself nor did any government department seek prior consultation to arrange for orderly and gradual cease-work procedure.
Then, further on he goes on to say:
Such drastic action would not have been necessary if there had been prior consultation and if the government had taken the company into its confidence, and advised us in advance of its intentions. This would have permitted an orderly and
Defence Policy, Planning and Production gradual adjustment of seniority and related staff problems and given employees a chance to seek other employment.
Still further, the president said:
Since the Prime Minister's original announcement September 23 which cast doubt on the future of the program, the company has repeatedly proposed to various government departments and even to Mr. Diefenbaker himself, alternate programs for the useful employment of the technical resources that have been assembled at Malton and which are second to none in the western world. However, the government has not seen fit to discuss these matters or consult with us in any way.
This is a statement which is in complete contradiction with what has already been said in this debate and, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) said, thus far it has not been contradicted. Therefore, again I put the question. Does the house think this is the way to sever the relationship between the government and this company? This is certainly not the way to deal with responsible private interests. There is no sharing here of confidence, as there should be. There is no opportunity to explore alternatives to the memorandum presented by the president of Avro to the Prime Minister on September 16, 1958.
I should like to deal for just a moment with the manner in which this contract was cancelled. I have in my hand the contract itself, or, I should say rather I have a form of contract with the Department of Defence Production which is "General Conditions DDP-26A", covering supplies. Section 26 is the termination clause of that contract. It states:
Notwithstanding anything in the contract contained the minister may, by giving notice to the contractor (hereinafter sometimes referred to as a "termination notice") terminate the contract as regards all or any part or parts of the work not theretofore completed. The minister may, at any time or from time to time, give one or more additional termination notices with respect to any or all parts of the work not terminated by any previous termination notice.
This is the termination clause. How was this contract terminated? I say that if the Prime Minister is right, that the September 23 statement is in itself a termination, that was quite an improper way to do it, and it is therefore unfair, unwarranted and improper on the part of the Prime Minister to suggest that the September statement was notice to the company. In fact, his statement did not affect in the slightest the obligations of Avro under the several contracts that it had with the Department of Defence Production, and until the formal notice was given, not in the house here but in the manner provided for under the contract and in the manner provided for under the Department

Defence Policy, Planning and Production of Defence Production Act for the termination of contracts, the contract was not terminated and that notice I submit was not given until February 20, 1959.
Let me go a step further. I hold in my hand the manual of procedure on termination of contracts with the Department of Defence Production and on page 10 of this manual, chapter II, there is a part dealing with the termination of the contracts.

speechtext:
The termination clause says:
All contracts placed by the Department of Defence Production contain a clause permitting termination or cancellation of the contract, or of the work called for by the contract, at any time, in whole or in part, by notice in writing by the minister.
Again I repeat, the minister did not give the notice. The Prime Minister says that he gave it. Now then, under the same chapter, continuing the effect of the termination clauses, we find this:
Upon receipt of a notice of termination, a contractor is required to cease work under the contract in accordance with and to the extent specified in the notice.
Here is the notice that was given to the company on February 20 by the Department of Defence Production, not by the minister as required. I quote from the notice:
Take notice that your contracts bearing the reference numbers set out below including all amendments thereto are hereby terminated as regards all supplies and services which have not been completed and shipped or performed thereunder prior to the receipt by you of this notice. You shall cease all work immediately, terminate subcontracts and orders, place no further subcontracts or orders and instruct all your subcontractors and suppliers to take similar action.
Could there be any clearer language than "you shall cease all work immediately, terminate subcontracts and orders and instruct all your subcontractors to take similar action"? What does the termination clause in the manual of procedure of the Department of Defence Production have to say with reference to that position? In it I find the following:

If the whole of the uncompleted portion of the contract is terminated, compliance with this requirement may involve cancellation of outstanding subcontracts and/or commitments for materials and parts, release of employees whose services are no longer required, or cancellation of contracts for the supply of power or other services.
So I say without any hesitation that the moment the company received this notice it had no other alternative but to do what it did, and that was to cease all work immediately. It had no other alternative but to diminish the claims which it might have for wages against the crown. It was its obligations and its responsibility so to do under the termination clause and certainly under the order which it received from the government. Not only that, but on Friday, February 20 when Avro had 14,000 men working they were told to cease work and if they had any of these men working after February 20 they would have no right to recover their wages from the crown except to the extent that their services were a necessary consequence of the termination. I have not heard it said in the house by anyone so far that the claim for wages that had been referred to would be a necessary termination of this contract. Therefore, though these employees were discharged on February 20 and although they are entitled to severance pay for three weeks, I believe the Prime Minister said, what I have pointed out follows as a consequence of the termination clause which I have put on the record.
The Prime Minister has stated in effect that the company took this action to embarrass the government. If you read the telegram you see that that is not the case. On the contrary, it was done by order of the government, on instructions received from the government and if the suggestion made on the other side of the house that the company should have kept these men on had been put into effect the company would have done so at its own expense and not at the expense of the crown as has been intimated in the debate. Therefore, the conclusion one must come to on this point is that before blaming the company and not the government for what happened on Friday, February 20 we must take cognizance of the following points. The government's decision was announced suddenly on February 20 instead of on March 31 as was expected.

speakeroldname: Hon. Raymond O'Hurley (Minister of Defence Production):
maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to commence on a rather humble note what is really my first speech in the house since my appointment as Minister of Defence Production. As I was appointed only in May last and have been obliged by illness on two different occasions to be absent from the House of Commons I do not pretend to know all the answers to production sharing nor do I pretend to know all the answers to defence production. You will perhaps like to know that it is a long distance from .my former occupation of forestry and wild life conservationist to the position I occupy today of Minister of Defence Production.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: It is still a wild life.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
It certainly is. But I think my past experience, although it was in a different field, serves me well in this new occupation.
The primary function of the Department of Defence Production is placing the contracts for the requirements of the Department of National Defence. For this reason naturally the two departments have worked and are working very closely together. My officials and the officials of the Department of National Defence are in daily discussions on matters of mutual interest. The complete accord reached by the two departments to extend this policy of production sharing and the work being done I think is a sign of success. Notwithstanding the gloomy picture portrayed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), we are optimistic as to the results we hope to obtain. For example, in order to denote the change of view in Washington I should like to be permitted to read and to have inserted in Hansard a press release from the Pentagon in Washington which proves just the opposite of what the


hon. gentleman referred to. The press release reads as follows:
U.S. Department of Defence Press Release,
February 23, 1959.
The air force announced today the signing of a contract by Boeing Airplane Company with Canadair Limited, Montreal, for the production of wings and ailerons for Bomarc missile.
The long range fully automatic Bomare missile is in quantity production for four U.S.A.F. bases already under construction in the northeastern United States. Ten additional Bomarc bases in the U.S. have been announced. The Canadian government has also decided to introduce the Bomarc into the Canadian air defence system. This was announced by the Prime Minister of Canada in September, 1958. The establishment of the Bomarc bases will be in accord with plans developed by the North American Air Defence Command (NORAD) for the defence of the North American continent. It is expected that in accordance with past practice the two governments will share the cost of the Bomarc installations in Canada which will be an integral part of the North American air defence system.
The Canadair contract is the first significant production contract awarded as a direct result of the production sharing effort agreed to after high level discussions between the two governments last year.
Due in part to the growing integration of Canadian and U.S. air defence, and in part to the high cost and technical complexity of modem defence equipment, both governments have recognized the desirability of moving toward a better utilization of their defence production capabilities.
This is from the Pentagon in Washington.
To this end, it is of great importance to North American defence that Canada as well as the United States maintain an industrial defence base capable of a significant contribution to the common defence and to the development of a fund of technology necessary to increasing productivity in the field of defence production.
It was jointly decided, therefore, to explore the possibility of closer co-operation between Canadian and U.S. industry in the production of weapon systems related to the defence of North America. Canadian industry has highly trained scientists, engineers and other skilled technicians and modern equipment, and it is expected that the increased emphasis on production co-ordination will result in greater utilization of Canadian defence production facilities by United States industrial and governmental procurement agencies in order to assure the most economical and effective use of the capabilities of both countries.
A series of conferences between Canadian and U.S. officials have been held during the last four months with a view to developing better co-operation in the production of defence weapons. The interdependence of Canada and the U.S. in defence matters was recognized in the Hyde Park declaration, April, 1941, and in the statement of principles for economic co-operation of October, 1950. The recent discussions have been carried out within the framework of these principles.
The immediate aim has been to utilize Canadian industrial capacity in the Bomarc, Sage and radar programs which are being financed jointly by both governments. Both governments are assisting inter-industry contact and facilitating exchange of information and personnel between American prime contractors and potential Canadian suppliers.
Interested American prime contractors have made visits to Canadian plants to obtain first-hand knowledge of their capabilities, and progress has been

made in having the names of Canadian firms placed on American industrial and governmental bidders' lists. Many companies have already submitted technical proposals and quotations, and several contracts have been placed on a competitive basis. It is expected that progress along these lines will continue.
Groups of officials are also looking beyond the immediate programs in order to work out effective arrangements for sharing the production of future defence equipment. To achieve this, the long term program must be based on Canada's ability to participate in co-ordinated development programs of mutual interest leading in time to production contracts. Studies are continuing in seeking areas of mutual interest in which a co-ordinated development effort is possible. Through proper long range planning in this manner, both governments feel the maximum use can be made of each country's skills and resources in the fulfilment of the common defence objectives of Canada and the United States.
That is a press release from the Pentagon in Washington.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to acquaint this house with the members of the joint Canada-United States production sharing committee who have held to date three general meetings. Might I add that there were meetings of a ministerial committee arranged by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the President of the United States one of which was held in Paris in December. The Canadian delegates of the joint Canada-United States production sharing committee were the deputy minister of the Department of Defence Production, Mr. Golden; Mr. Miller, deputy minister of the Department of National Defence; Mr. LePan, who has taken another position, assistant undersecretary of state for external affairs; and Mr. MacNeill, assistant secretary of treasury board. The United States delegates were: the assistant secretary (material) United States air force, who was chairman; the assistant secretary (logistics) United States army; and the assistant secretary (material) United States navy. The meetings held by this committee were on October 9, 1958, November 18, 1958 and February 10, 1959.
Between these meetings, members of the different departments have been holding continual discussions and meetings. Only this afternoon three members of my department left for Washington and other parts of the United States in connection with this program of production sharing and the removal of different objections mentioned by the member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) which hampered -I will deal with this situation later-the ease by which the Canadian contractors can obtain work from the United States.
I wish here to give some outline of the work that is being done in my department to bring production sharing into effect, not only as pieces of paper but so that our contractors in Canada can share in the gigantic defence
Defence Policy, Planning and Production program which is going on in the United States. One of the first major tasks in increasing the opportunities for Canadian industry to share in the production of military equipment for the United States has been to familiarize United States procurement agencies and the prime contractors with Canadian industrial capabilities; and, secondly, to arrange for Canadian industry to quote on current military requirements. On the Bomarc missile program considerable progress has occurred in the last three months.
First of all, facility capability reports on 63 Canadian industrial concerns have been forwarded by the Department of Defence Production to the Boeing airplane company in Seattle. Secondly, under the auspices of the Department of Defence Production senior Boeing officials have visited about 50 Canadian companies throughout Canada for on the spot investigation of their capabilities. Over 45 Canadian companies have sent representatives to Boeing for a thorough briefing on the Bomarc weapon system. Boeing has issued over 170 invitations to tender to 77 Canadian companies. Many tenders have already been submitted and are presently being evaluated. Similar arrangements are being made with the major United States subcontractors to Boeing in instances where Bomarc work had already been contracted for. These companies are in turn exploring the areas where they can subcontract some of the work into Canada.
With the Sage and radar improvement programs opportunities for production sharing are not as extensive, but do represent a very significant dollar potential in the fields of radar, communications and data processing equipment. Four major United States prime contractors along with procurement specialists from the United States air force have undertaken extensive tours of potential industrial sources in Canada. In all, over 50 electronic and electro-mechanical companies have been visited in the last three months. Over 25 Canadian firms have visited a like number of United States firms and government procurement agencies in the same time period. Eighty invitations to tender have been received. Over 50 of these have resulted in Canadian bids being submitted, and these are now being evaluated.
The efforts of the government to improve the knowledge of the United States as to our capabilities and increasing the opportunities for Canadian industry to quote have not been restricted to the Bomarc, Sage and radar programs. A number of other programs of mutual interest are being examined. United States prime contractors involved in these programs are being approached by Canadian government and industrial personnel. We are

Defence Policy, Planning and Production being assisted in these endeavours by the United States military departments who are giving every encouragement to the United States companies to share with Canadian industry the development and production of military equipments for which they have been given contractual responsibility.
Mr. Speaker, I wish at this point to acquaint this house with the fact that the Department of Defence Production has sent invitations to Canadian concerns who have the capabilities to tender on defence programs, and we are ready and willing in the department to proceed to arrange interviews for them, to brief them on how to tender, and advise them on the material which is best suited to any given tender. The Department of Defence Production is working extensively on this problem of helping Canadian contractors.

These invitations were sent out in the month of December. The hon. member for Laurier in making his speech very rightly said that there were several impediments to getting contracts from the United States. In our department we call them road blocks. He mentioned a few of them, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will mention several more road blocks, about which I am glad to say progress is being made. I can truthfully say to the house that several of these road blocks to Canadian production sharing are being constantly removed, and we are quite optimistic on a final result being obtained.
Procedural and administrative road blocks in the United States are receiving the active attention of senior officials of the Canadian and United States governments with a view to a liberalization of United States procurement policies and procedures. In this manner Canadian firms will have a better opportunity to compete on an equal footing with United States firms for defence production in programs of mutual interest. Considerable progress has been made toward the removal of hindrances to production sharing which existed during the days of the former government.
Some of the impediments which are being removed, and some of the relaxations now permitted may be listed as follows:
1.	The "Buy American" act as applied to United States defence purchasing in Canada.
2.	Duty free entry to the United States of Canadian defence material.

3.	Qualification approval of Canadian manufactured equipment such as electronic components.
4.	Security restrictions which in the past have prevented Canadian firms from participating in classified United States projects.
5.	Transmission to Canada of United States technical information in order that Canadian firms might be better qualified to quote on United States defence requirements.
6.	Easier negotiation of licensing agreements between United States companies and the Canadian government or its contractors in order to permit the manufacture in Canada of United States designed equipment.
Reticence on the part of the United States defence industry has always existed in the past with regard to subcontracting work to Canadian firms. Through the active co-operation of the United States military departments, United States industry is being made aware of production sharing arrangements between Canada, and the United States and are being assisted in every way to assess our capabilities and to place more defence work in Canada. This will take some time, but already significant results are occurring. I have here a list of contracts which have been carried out in Canada. These are known major United States subcontracts placed in Canada in the last four to five months.

Several of these contracts have already been submitted to the prime contractors in the United States and I have every hope, judging from the results already obtained that the Canadian manufacturers have a good chance of obtaining a number of these contracts.
In past years there was a program of production sharing during the construction of the radar lines. I wish to be quite clear, and to say quite frankly that I am speaking now of engineering work in the electronic field; I am not speaking of construction or of air transport. Under the United States air force radar augmentation and gap filler project referred to in diplomatic note No. D-155 and No. D-156, dated June 1955, the Canadian

government reaffirmed the principle that electronic equipment at installations on Canadian territory should as far as practicable, be manufactured in Canada, the factors to be taken into account would include availability at the time required, cost and performance.
Of a total of nine stations having a total equipment value of $10 million, Canada obtained only $75,000 for installation, having stated, with regard to the equipment that it was not practicable for Canadian industry to deliver on time. In view of the urgent nature of program 572, which concerned preliminary site surveys and the construction of two trial sites for the D.E.W. line, Canada waived participation. The total estimated cost of this project, which is referred to in the diplomatic note No. 163, was $29 million.
Under the terms of diplomatic note No. 306 of May 1955 the terms governing the practicability of D.E.W. line construction were similar to those contained in previous notes and included such considerations as availability at the time required, cost and performance. Of an estimated cost of electronic equipment of more than $125 million, Canadian industry share was $10 million. With regard to project Dewdrop, involving a radio communication system from Cape Dyer north across Thule, Greenland, similar terms were agreed as referred to in diplomatic note No. 158 of July 1957. Because time was short, Canadian Arms were unable to participate in the supply of electronic equipment needed for this project, the cost of which was estimated at $10 million.
It was obvious that the practicability clauses used by the former government were not proving effective and therefore the present government had to consider alternative arrangements in order to accomplish the desired objectives. Hon. members who consider the content of the diplomatic notes I have just read will see that we obtained only $10 million out of an estimated total of $175 million, or only 5.7 per cent of the contracts awarded.
At this point I should like to turn to the question of the Arrow. The Leader of the Opposition suggested that the proper time to have begun discussions with the United States regarding the sale of the Arrow to the United States air force was in October, 1957. He stated that the unveiling ceremony conducted at the Avro plant would have been an appropriate time at which to have raised this question. I suggest that this statement clearly indicates the bankruptcy of ideas of the former government with respect to production and cost sharing with the United States. Surely the proper time to have initiated such discussions was during the
Defence Policy, Planning and Production early stages of the program in 1952 and 1953. If proper cost and production sharing discussions had been held at that time the Arrow weapon system might have become a common requirement of both the United States and of the R.C.A.F. The fact is that it was too late, as we ultimately found out, to interest the United States government in this aircraft, because their own plans for aircraft in the interceptor category had been made. What we are now attempting to do in the production and cost sharing field is what should have been done years ago.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes)-and I wish in passing, to thank him very kindly for the assistance he gave me in his speech this afternoon-fully explored the possibilities of selling the Arrow to the United States. As I have indicated, it was too late. Never will this government enter into a program of such magnitude as the one just ended without prior discussions with our allies on production and cost sharing.

speechtext:
I listened with great interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Laurier about the termination of the Avro contract. The hon. gentleman read part 1 of the termination clauses. If he had read part 2 he would have found that it says: "... to proceed with any portion of the work which is not terminated." We did not terminate work on the production of spares and overhaul for the CF-100. We did not terminate the program which Avro has under way for the United States. We did not terminate at the Orenda works the program for production of Orenda engine spares and overhaul. When the termination notice was given it was the intention of the Department of Defence Production that the other programs should continue and that the men should be maintained at their work or on leave of absence under the labour contracts. As I say, we have not cancelled the contracts for the production of CF-100 spares and Orenda has a contract on hand from the West German government worth $6 million. The CF-100 spare contract amounts to $10 million for this current year-money which should be spent by March 31-while there is a further amount of some $3 million in

Defence Policy, Planning and Production respect of Orenda engine spares which is not already spent and which should be spent by March 31.
There was still work to be done and the company should have had every reason to continue to employ certain of their employees. The reason given by the company was that they did not have on hand the seniority list of those they should keep on according to the labour contracts. It is a requirement under a union contract that a company must have for the inspection of the labour department up to date seniority lists. I cannot justify the position the company took in letting everyone out as soon as they got notice of the cancellation of the Arrow program.

But if it is true that the company had no inkling whatever that the contract was going to be terminated how is it that I should have copies of letters going back over the months, exchanged between the Avro company and my department containing references to termination costs?
At the company's insistence negotiations were entered into during 1957 regarding the termination procedures to be followed concerning capital equipment and other matters. These negotiations lasted over a period of many months and were only partially concluded at the time of termination. In letters from Orenda dated October 27, 1958, and from Avro dated October 22, 1958, reference was made to termination. I quote specifically from a letter dated January 27, 1958 addressed to my deputy minister:
However, and in accordance with our normal practice as previously mentioned, both companies will have further substantial outstanding commitments at that time, and the purpose of this letter is to draw this matter formally to your attention and obtain your recognition of this fact, so that in the event of termination the actual expenditures arising therefrom which are deemed to be reasonably and properly incurred, will be recognized and reimbursed by your department.
And again I quote from a letter dated February 9 to the Minister of Public Works


(Mr. Green) who served as acting minister of defence production whilst I was ill:
My purpose in writing you, therefore, is to state that we are carrying on the work in accordance with what we understand to be your wishes, notwithstanding the literal provisions of the contracts, and on the assumption that the reasonable and proper costs incurred will be reimbursed in the event of termination.
The charge has been made that the current defence production policy is permitting our trained engineers and technicians to leave Canadian industry for the United States and elsewhere. I would like to point out that upon termination of the Astra and Sparrow projects arrangements were made with some ten firms to retain a nucleus of their engineering teams totalling some 300 personnel until such time as other work could be obtained as a result of United States-Canada production sharing activities.
In the case of the CF-105 cancellation the house is aware of the arrangements which are proposed with Avro and Orenda companies to retain a number of their skilled technicians until such time as other useful work of a commercial or defence nature may be found for them.
The Leader of the Opposition this afternoon implied that the cancellation of the Arrow has resulted in the destruction of the aircraft industry in Canada. I would like to correct this erroneous impression.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the hon. minister corrects that impression may I be permitted to say that I made no such statement during the course of my remarks this afternoon as he will discover when he reads Hansard.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I shall take the hon. member's word in this respect but I believe he strongly implied that the industry had been adversely affected. May I be permitted to go on to state that Avro and Orenda are today in operation with 20 per cent of the manpower they employed at the time of termination carrying out their other contracts for the government which are of a continuing nature. Avro also holds contracts from the United States air force and the United States army for the development and prototyping of a vertical take-off aircraft, which appears at this time to have considerable potential and may develop into a long range development program.
Canadair Limited in Montreal are presently occupied building the Argus CC-107; the long range transport CC-106 and the turboprop Cosmopolitan CC-109. The latter two are passenger transport aircraft and show promise of developing into excellent commercial sales.

In addition Canadair are supporting the F-86 Sabre and the T-33 trainer, both with spares and repair operations. This company has also successfully supplied spares support to aircraft utilized by the U.S. air force.
At De Havilland Limited the development of the Caribou is progressing extremely well and a production line has been started. At the same time De Havilland are continuing to produce Beavers and Otters for commercial and military sales. The CS-2F, the R.C.N. tracker, continues to employ a large labour force at De Havilland with subcontracts at Bristol, Winnipeg; Canadian Car, Fort William; Fleet Manufacturing, Fort Erie, and Enamel and Heat in Amherst, Nova Scotia.
Canadian Pratt & Whitney are continuing to produce the R-1820 engine installed in the CS-2F for the R.C.N. as well as supplying spares for existing engines both in Canada and the United States. In 1958 their sales in spare parts only to the United States amounted to over $11 million. This firm also provides a large employment of personnel to support the repair and overhaul of service aircraft and helicopters.
Rolls Royce Limited are continuing to support the Nene engine powering the T-33 aircraft and will service and repair Tyne engines for use in the CC-106 cargo transport aircraft. Here again the firm enjoys a large commercial program and is not wholly dependent on defence contracts.
Behind these major contractors in the aircraft industry is a network of subcontractors and suppliers in support. These cover every phase of aircraft production and although some will be affected by the termination of the Arrow the majority of them are diversified enough to be able to continue in a relatively strong position.
There are many other companies engaged in the repair and overhaul of service aircraft, many of whom contribute to the production programs. Although the strength of the industry has been depleted it is still a very healthy industry and will continue to be so.
The suggestion has been made that the present policy of defence production is resulting in a sellout to the United States. I would like to correct this erroneous impression by giving the house the figures for the calendar year 1958. Of a total of $730 million in defence contracts placed during that year only 3 per cent thereof or $20 million was placed outside Canada and of this amount only $10 million net represents contracts placed directly in the United States. Here I would also like to note that with respect to the moneys spent by my department, 92 per cent is spent here in Canada.
Defence Policy, Planning and Production
The Leader of the Opposition has challenged me to state what is the policy of the Canadian government with respect to defence production. The policy of the Canadian government is to maintain a production industry capable of providing the requirements of the Canadian forces, while at the same time utilizing the production resources of our allies where appropriate and making available to our allies our production resources where appropriate. Although this policy must be flexible enough to meet changing conditions, it is in essence the same policy pursued by the previous government, of which the Leader of the Opposition was a member, the difference being that now we want and are achieving more results in the fields of production sharing.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to engage in this debate on the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition. I should like to read it to remind hon. members of what is under debate at the present time. The amendment reads:
This house regrets that the prolonged delay of the government in determining air defence policy and planning in co-operation with our allies is preventing the effective use of Canada's defence production facilities and manpower.
I am honoured to follow the Minister of Defence Production in this debate but I must say at the outset that I was disappointed in his reading of his statement in the last 45 minutes because, in my opinion, he gave us very little in his elaboration of what he said last Monday after the affair of the Arrow had occurred on the previous Friday when he had occasion to make his statement in the house.
I am not rising to speak on this matter because I feel that I have technical knowledge of the various angles of the problem involved; but as I left my area of the Nickel Belt last night my people asked me to take part in the debate, if the occasion arose, concerning the catastrophe which has occurred in the aircraft industry in Canada, and I am pleased to do that on their behalf. It was said last week by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) that the effects of the breakdown of the Arrow contracts and program upon the aircraft industry will be felt in the not too distant future by many industries and citizens of Canada. With that in mind I am sure that the people of the Nickel Belt realize the effect that it will have on the production of nickel which was necessarily involved in the production of the Arrow.
This amendment was placed before the house for the purpose of discussing possibly two things, namely the merits of the action taken by the government on the one hand

Defence Policy, Planning and Production and on the other the method by which the government proceeded to achieve the decision which it made a very short while ago. Since I am not a specialist I do not wish to, and I do not think that I could, cope with the problem of the merits of the question of the cancelling of the Arrow contract, although I realize that every member in the house would expect the government to make its decision with all the information possible in hand. Later on we may not be pleased to realize that our government, with all the information at its disposal, made a wrong decision. The matter under discussion, is the obvious method used by the Conservative government in dealing with this problem. It is a method which has shown up in every problem which this Conservative government has been called upon to solve since I became a member of this house for the first time.
There is one problem that possibly the Canadian people felt this government could solve with some knowledge, and that was the problem of the Arrow. As I see it, the problem is simple. The government had to make a decision and probably they made the right decision. It had to think of the conversion of the utilities of that great industry; it had to think of the diversion of the utilities which that industry could continue to give to Canada. In these two fields this government has shown itself as a specialist both in conversion and diversion. On the other hand, I know that the Canadian people, as they inquire, as they read the newspapers, realize that, as on other occasions, this government has fumbled the ball and has not brought about the solution which the citizens and the taxpayers should expect from this government. I will attempt to prove that, Mr. Speaker. This is not just a loose saying on my part.
What was the attitude of the government?

I hear laughter. There are many interjections by our Conservative friends, but I am amazed to learn that most of them interject when a member of the opposition is speaking. They should take their turns, and if they have opinions on this very grave matter they should tell the government. They are entitled to take their turns. There are many interjections, mostly when members of the opposition are discussing important matters.
What occurred when this was first announced in the house? It was indicated that there was no problem at all. It was not a grave problem; it was well in hand. That was the first indication regarding this matter by the Prime Minister himself and the members of the government. That has been the

attitude taken on many other grave problems in Canada since I have been a member of this house. I could mention the matter of coal which was brought up in the house. That was the attitude of the government at that time and that is the attitude today. An attempt was made to adjourn the house to discuss the matter of coal but we were not successful.
Once the opposition made it clear that there were grave problems about the method by which this decision was made we were told, as we have been told on many occasions when important matters have been discussed, that the people had made a decision last March; that there were 208 Conservative members in this house and that was a good enough answer to any problem which the Canadian people may have. You can read the debates. I heard the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) say that that is not true. He can read the speeches made by the members of the government last Monday and if he does he will find that this matter of the majority was brought up once again.
We all know that the CF-105 was cancelled. The suggestion was that the government would like to replace it with the PC-208. That is roughly the suggestion. I feel it is a very limited argument, and we do hear it very often in this house and that it will take care of the Canadian people; that they had an opportunity last March and we know what they did with that opportunity, Mr. Speaker. I think that today, and especially on the morrow of this decision of the government concerning the Arrow contract and the method by which it was terminated, the Canadian people are disappointed and they would favour an opportunity of using the ballot to deal with the PC-208.
What is the government's attitude concerning the Arrow problem? I have dealt with the first two matters. There is a third attitude, the attitude of "so what". We can well recall that when the major Canadian problem of unemployment was being dealt with in the house at another time over many weeks and months the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), the junior Minister without Portfolio, said with respect to unemployment, "so what"? We heard the same words again not long ago in the house when the grave problem with respect to coal in the eastern provinces was brought to the attention of hon. members. What did we hear? We heard the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) indicate that there was no such thing.

Then we come to the Arrow project. We can all read the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to see what he thinks about that. His attitude was "so what" too, that there was no problem except the problem created by the company. That is the way the government takes upon its shoulders the responsibilities given to the government by the Canadian people with a very large majority last March. The government says that there is no responsibility on their shoulders concerning the aircraft industry and their future, that it is all on the shoulders of the company. It is surprising that the Prime Minister would make such a statement when on the day following the announcement of cancellation the president of Avro had this to say:
Such drastic action would not have been necessary if there had been prior consultation and if the government had taken the company into its confidence and advised us in advance of its intentions. This would have permitted an orderly and gradual adjustment of seniority and related staff problems and given employees a chance to seek other employment.
That is what the president of the company had to say. We were told only a few moments ago by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) that the discussions which should have taken place were considered only on the very day of the announcement. That is a confession by the Minister of Defence Production himself. What is the answer as to the policy and attitude of the government concerning this grave decision? It is obvious. Absolutely no assurance was given to the house of any sign of preparedness before the announcement was made.
To indicate that this is so I should like to refer to what was said by the Minister of Defence Production tonight. He said the government is confident that something could well occur and that the government has extended invitations. Everything is in the future but for the last week the Canadian people have known that the decision is in the past and proper action should have been taken before the decision instead of extending invitations for the future tonight.
In his statement of a week ago the Minister of Defence Production said in the first paragraph that a Canada-United States ministerial committee on joint defence has been
Defence Policy, Planning and Production established. That is what he said last week. I recall the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) indicating some time ago that the specialty of the government was to study the possibility of instituting a committee to study something. That is the process which has been used in this case. We come to the second paragraph of the statement of the Minister of Defence Production where we find the following:
A committee of senior officials of Canada and the United States has been established to deal with the development and production sharing aspects of our military requirements.
Again something in the future, something in the realm of study only. Then we come to paragraph four where we find these words:
We are now determined to make these existing agreements effective in action.
Again something in the future. Here is what we find in paragraph five:
Both governments are helping to establish better inter-industry contact than has existed in the past.
More political talk. Something in the future, nothing concrete. What do we find is the minister's conclusion? He places the burden of solving the problem on someone else's shoulders, for in his statement he says:
The real success of production sharing endeavours depends, to a large degree, upon the determination of Canadian industry vigorously to seek defence business in the United States either as prime or as subcontractors.
There is the measure of the policy of the government, to have industry take the entire load. We also have the statement made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes). His words were in part confusing to me and certainly to many other members of the house. When he spoke last week he made reference to the money involved. On this score I will only say that I do not criticize the decision. I hope it was the proper one. I feel that the government may have made the proper decision, but in reading his speech again after listening to it I see that he was concerned with the money involved. If one couples that with the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and puts two and two together I fear that when the budget is brought down we will find that the defence of Canada possibly has been used to satisfy another portfolio.
